introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: three and a quarter hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR QUESTIONS in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each. Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references. Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed. Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and Two outline maps of Cameroon.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions in all : question ONE (obligatoire, 31 marks), ONE question de la Section B et TWO de la Section C ». `regles_choix` porte le minimum exprimable par section (B : 1 sur 2 ; C : 2 sur 4) ; la question 1 (Section A) est obligatoire donc sans règle ; la consigne complète (4 questions en tout) est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : Q1 = 31 (5+6+4+4+6+4+2), Q2 à Q7 = 23 chacune (Q2 : 4+2+3+4+5+3+2 ; Q3 : 12+3+5+3 ; Q4 : 5+10+8 ; Q5 : 6+(8+3)+6 ; Q6 : 6+10+7 ; Q7 : 8+6+9), soit 100 points pour les 4 questions à traiter ; aucun écart avec les totaux imprimés. Pour les blocs à plusieurs items (Q1 a, b, c ; Q5 b), `points` de la sous-question est la somme des points imprimés des items.

Sujet scanné de 5 pages (page de garde, questions 1 à 7, carte topographique de Ndop avec sa légende, fond de carte du Cameroun) ; filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. La carte (pivotée de 90 degrés sur la page, remise à l'endroit) et le fond de carte SONT dans le PDF et ont été recadrés en PNG ; le papier millimétré n'est pas fourni.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level. Aucune statistique précise n'est avancée sauf celles du tableau imprimé de la Q3 ; les ordres de grandeur (pluviométries, altitudes, dates de création d'organismes ou de lois) sont donnés prudemment et sont à faire relire par un géographe avant mise en avant.

Q1 : la carte de Ndop est un scan de qualité moyenne (basse résolution, pli central vers l'Easting 55-56, texte souvent illisible). Les descriptions (relief plus élevé et plus disséqué à l'ouest de l'Easting 56, plaine à pentes douces et terrains marécageux à l'est, escarpement hachuré vers le Northing 41 à l'ouest, route goudronnée dans le nord, symbole de rizière dans le sud-ouest de la plaine) sont lues sur le scan ; les altitudes citées (environ 1 150 à 1 200 m à l'est, plus de 1 200 m à l'ouest) sont des ordres de grandeur lus sur des cotes partiellement lisibles ; les toponymes cités (Ndop, Bamessing, Babanki Tungo, Balikumbat) sont ceux qui se lisent sur le scan ; à vérifier sur la carte originale.

Q1 : l'échelle imprimée est 1:50 000 (1 km = 2 cm) mais le scan réduit la carte sur une page A4 (un carreau de la grille mesure environ 1,3 cm sur le scan) : le corrigé fait mesurer les distances avec les carreaux de 1 km de la grille et non avec une règle appliquée au scan.

Q1(c)(i) : les références à six chiffres sont lues 631440 = Easting 63,1 / Northing 44,0 et 646400 = Easting 64,6 / Northing 40,0. La longueur du chenal (environ 5,5 km) est mesurée sur le scan par un tracé polygonal (figure schématique, origine « corrige ») : elle donne un indice de sinuosité d'environ 1,3 ; la mesure au fil sur la carte originale peut donner 1,25 à 1,35. Le corrigé le dit et donne la méthode.

Défauts d'impression du sujet : « iin » (Q1 b i), « practicing » ; le tableau de la Q3 indique « Rainfall in cm » alors que les valeurs (104 à 279) ne sont réalistes qu'en millimètres pour Kuala Lumpur (total annuel 2 406) : transcrit tel qu'imprimé, le corrigé trace les valeurs imprimées et signale l'unité probable ; « Edtion » et « Certificate Physical and Human Geography » dans la source ; la Q3 (b) se termine par « a) above.. » ; les libellés du fond de carte portent « 100°E » (probablement 10°E) et « 2°N » à l'extrémité sud ; le fond de carte est annoncé « for questions 4, 5, 6 and 7 » ; la Q5 (a) imprime « analyse their resources » (formulation inhabituelle pour de la végétation, conservée telle quelle). Aucun point imprimé n'est corrigé.

Q2 : question de travail de terrain à réponse personnelle : le corrigé est un modèle générique suivant le thème (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, avec les équivalents pour les cinq autres thèmes ; aucune donnée réelle n'est avancée, les valeurs numériques (largeur 2,4 m, profondeur 0,3 m, vitesse 0,5 m/s) sont purement illustratives et signalées comme telles. Le thème (iv) « Functional segregation » est recopié tel qu'imprimé.

Q3 : climogramme (figure 1, origine « corrige ») tracé avec les valeurs imprimées (axe de pluie gradué en « cm » comme imprimé). Total annuel 2 406 ; température moyenne 26,4 °C ; amplitude 1 °C (recalculés par script).

Q4(a) : les basses terres et hautes terres traversées par la Ligne volcanique du Cameroun (Mont Cameroun, Bamenda Highlands pour les reliefs ; plaine de Ndop, plaine de Tikar, plaine de Mbo pour les basses terres) sont des réponses usuelles de cours ; d'autres choix valables sont possibles. Q4(c) cite UNVDA (Upper Noun Valley Development Authority), SEMRY, IRAD, CamCCUL, MINADER, les ordonnances foncières de 1974 : institutions réelles mais dates et résultats volontairement non détaillés.

Q5 à Q7 : exemples réels reconnus (Mont Cameroun, Parc national de Waza, chutes de la Lobé et plages de Kribi, palais de Foumban et de Bafut, jardin botanique de Limbe, Edéa, Song Loulou, Lagdo, SONARA, ALUCAM, SOSUCAM, CICAM, Société nationale d'investissement, zones franches, complexe industrialo-portuaire de Kribi, FEICOM, Douala et Logone pour les inondations). Aucun chiffre précis (production, dates exactes, effectifs) n'est avancé ; le fond de carte est décrit (zones de végétation) mais aucune carte de végétation n'est tracée.

questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Using a sketch map, locate the area of your fieldwork investigation. *(4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**What to write.** Name the exact place, then fix it from the large scale to the small scale, and add a neat sketch map.
1. *Administrative location:* region, division and nearest town or village, with the distance and direction from it (for example, "a stream about 3 km north-east of the school, in X Division").
2. *Geographical location:* approximate latitude and longitude or a grid reference, and the position relative to a main road, river, hill or other feature.
3. *Setting:* altitude, relief, climate, vegetation or land use of the site, which show why it was suitable.
4. *Sketch map:* a small map with a frame, the main roads, the stream or site and the sampling points, a north arrow, a scale, a key and a title; a small inset map of Cameroon with the region shaded.

**Marking guide.** Administrative position 1, relative position or distance 1, coordinates or grid reference 1, annotated sketch map 1. A vague statement ("near my town") earns at most 1 mark.

**Equivalents for the other topics.** (i) Vegetation: name the forest or savanna patch, its altitude and soil. (ii) Coastal processes: name the beach or cliff, the sea, the direction of the waves. (iv) Functional segregation: name the town and the zone studied (central business district, residential area). (v) and (vi): name the urban or rural area, with its quarters or villages.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) State your objective and hypothesis that guided your investigation of the topic. *(2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**Model (topic iii).**
- *Objective (1 mark):* to find out how the characteristics of a stream channel (width, depth, velocity and discharge) change downstream.
- *Hypothesis (1 mark):* **the discharge (and the channel width, depth and velocity) of the stream increases downstream.** A hypothesis is a testable statement which can be accepted or rejected with the data; it must not be a question.

**Equivalents.** (i) "Tree height and species diversity change with altitude (or distance from the forest edge)." (ii) "Beach pebbles become smaller and rounder with distance along the beach in the direction of longshore drift." (iv) "Land use zones are segregated: shops and offices are concentrated in the centre and housing at the edge." (v) "Land use changes with distance from the town centre, from commercial use to residential." (vi) "Land use depends on the distance from the village and the slope."

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) State the significance of the tools you used in the investigation. *(3 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**Model (topic iii): tool, use, significance (1 mark each for three well explained tools).**
| Tool | Use | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Measuring tape and ranging poles | Width of the channel, spacing of the sites | Gives accurate, standard measurements of distance and width, so that sites can be compared. |
| Metre rule (or depth stick) | Depth at regular intervals across the channel | Gives the cross-sectional area, which is needed for discharge. |
| Float (orange or cork) and stopwatch | Time the float over a fixed distance to find the velocity | A cheap and simple way to measure the speed of the flow where there is no current meter. |
| Clinometer, calipers, field notebook, GPS or map | Slope, pebble size, recording and locating | Show the gradient and bedload size and make the results reliable and repeatable. |

**General point.** Each tool is chosen because it is simple, cheap, accurate enough for school fieldwork and the readings can be repeated and compared; the weakness is the human error (for example, the float is slowed by the wind).

**Equivalents.** Vegetation: quadrat, tape, transect line, clinometer, soil auger, identification key. Coasts: ranging poles, clinometer, calipers, tape. Urban or rural land use: base map, questionnaire, pedestrian counter, field sheet.

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Describe how your data was collected. *(4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**Model (topic iii).**
1. *Pilot survey and site selection (1 mark):* a stretch of the stream was visited first and **three or more sites** were chosen at intervals downstream (for example, 500 m apart), using a systematic sampling approach, a safe place with a straight, uniform channel.
2. *Width and depth (1 mark):* at each site the tape was stretched across the channel from bank to bank; the depth was measured with a metre rule at regular points (for example, every 20 cm) across the channel.
3. *Velocity (1 mark):* a float was released upstream, timed with a stopwatch over a measured distance (for example, 10 m) three times and the average taken; the surface speed was multiplied by a correction factor (about 0.8) to obtain a mean velocity.
4. *Other data (1 mark):* the bedload size (for example, the longest axis of 10 pebbles), the roundness, the gradient with a clinometer, all noted in a field notebook; the work was done in teams, with roles assigned, on the same day and under similar weather.

**Equivalents.** Vegetation: transect and quadrats, counting species and measuring height. Coastal processes: beach profile with ranging poles and clinometer, pebble sampling. Land use: mapping by field survey and counting functions, questionnaires to a random or systematic sample of residents or farmers.

questions.enonce_markdown: (e) How was data analyzed and presented? *(5 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**Model (topic iii).**

*Analysis (about 3 marks).*
- Mean values were calculated for width, depth and velocity at each site.
- The cross-sectional area was found as width x mean depth, then the **discharge** as $Q = A \times v$. *Illustration only:* width 2.4 m, mean depth 0.3 m, velocity 0.5 m/s give $A = 2.4 \times 0.3 = 0.72\ \text{m}^2$ and $Q = 0.72 \times 0.5 = 0.36\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$. The wetted perimeter and the hydraulic radius ($R = A/P$) may also be calculated.
- A statistical test such as **Spearman's rank correlation coefficient** between distance downstream and discharge was used to test the hypothesis, using the formula $r_s = 1 - \dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2 - 1)}$ and the table of significance for $n$ sites.

*Presentation (about 2 marks).*
- Tables of the field data.
- Cross-section diagrams of the channel at each site, drawn on graph paper to scale.
- A long profile or a line graph of velocity or discharge against distance downstream, and a scatter graph of discharge and distance with a line of best fit.
- Annotated field sketches and photographs, and a map of the sites.

**Equivalents.** Vegetation: transect diagram and kite diagram, bar charts of species. Coasts: beach profile, pebble size and roundness graphs. Land use: land use map (choropleth or colour shading), bar charts, the percentage of each land use, the nearest-neighbour or the Spearman test.

questions.enonce_markdown: (f) What were your findings in relation to the hypothesis and conclusion? *(3 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**Model (topic iii).** *Illustrative findings; a real candidate must use real results.*
- *Findings (1 mark):* width, depth, velocity and discharge generally **increased downstream**, because more tributaries joined the channel and the channel became smoother; the pebbles became smaller and rounder because of attrition. One site (for example, a rocky section or a place after a tributary) did not follow the trend.
- *Hypothesis (1 mark):* the Spearman coefficient was positive and above the critical value at the chosen significance level, so the **hypothesis was accepted** (if the coefficient was below the critical value it would be rejected, and that is an equally valid result).
- *Conclusion (1 mark):* the stream behaves as the theory of the Bradshaw model predicts; the weak points (small sample of sites, human error, a single day of measurement, the influence of rainfall) are mentioned, together with how the investigation could be improved (more sites, repeated measurements).

questions.enonce_markdown: (g) Of what importance was the fieldwork result to your community? *(2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Model answer: the candidate must answer from his or her own fieldwork. The model below follows one complete enquiry, topic (iii) Channel flow/characteristics, and gives the equivalent points for the other five topics. Any numerical values are illustrative only, not data from a real survey.*

**Model (topic iii), 2 marks for two developed points.**
- The knowledge of the discharge and of the flood level helps the community to plan the location of **bridges, culverts, water intakes and wells**, and to avoid building in the flood zone.
- It shows how much water can be used for **domestic use, irrigation, fish ponds or micro hydro** without drying the stream, and it can guide farmers on water use.
- The pupils acquire skills in measurement and teamwork, and the data can be handed to the local council or school for future comparison.

**Equivalents.** Vegetation: protection of the forest, firewood use and conservation. Coasts: coastal protection and tourism planning. Urban and rural land use: planning of markets, roads and housing; farming improvement.
